vignette:
Rosa's Vignette

Rosa was thirty-nine when she came to her first appointment, her hands folded tightly in her lap, her wedding ring catching the light as she turned it around and around her finger. She had been married to Miguel for fourteen years, and it was only now, three years after the assault, that she had finally agreed to talk to someone. The reason was simple and crushing: Miguel had stopped asking her to come to bed with him. He had stopped asking anything at all.

The assault had happened on a Tuesday evening in late October, in the parking garage beneath the nonprofit where Rosa worked as a program director. She had stayed late to finish grant applications—a habit, she would later think, that had made her weak, had made her predictable, had made her the kind of woman who would be alone in a concrete stairwell at seven o'clock. A man with a knife had cornered her between the second and third level. She could see the blade—a kitchen knife, she thought, though the sequence of what happened next remained fractured in her mind, pieces that would not fit together in any order that made sense. There was the cold wall. There was her own voice, which she could not quite hear. There was the feeling of her clothes being torn, and then the feeling of not being clothed, of being exposed in a way that made her skin feel like it did not belong to her. When she tried to tell Miguel what happened, the words would not come. She knew—she could see it all, somehow, even though she could not arrange it—but her mouth would open and nothing would arrive. The rage came instead. When she tried to speak about it in the following weeks, she would feel a heat rising in her chest, a fury so complete that she would have to leave the room.

For the first year, Rosa had convinced herself she was managing. She went back to work. She showered with the bathroom door locked and the shower curtain drawn. But by the second year, the nights had become unbearable. She would lie awake beside Miguel, listening to him breathe, certain that the darkness held something dangerous. During the day, with light coming through the windows, she could almost believe the world was ordinary. But as soon as the sun began to lower, her body would tighten. She found herself checking locks three, four, five times. She could not sit with her back to a door. When Miguel would reach for her in bed, she would flinch so violently that he stopped reaching.

The triggers were everywhere, though she had not named them that way until recently. A knife on the kitchen counter—even Miguel's butter knife—would send her heart racing. A news report showing violence would make her leave the room. But the worst was a particular moment each week: Saturday mornings at the community center, where Rosa used to lead a women's group focused on cultural traditions and mutual support. She had not gone in over two years. Her abuela had called three times asking why she no longer came. Her sister had stopped inviting her to family gatherings. Rosa had come to believe that she had forfeited her place in the community, that weakness was visible on her, that any other woman would have fought differently, would have prevented this, would not have been so stupid as to stay late in an empty building. She had become someone she did not recognize—someone isolated, someone her own family was learning to live without.

When Miguel finally said, quietly, that he thought she should talk to someone, Rosa felt something crack open. She was terrified of what speaking would require. But she was more terrified of losing him entirely, of becoming the kind of woman who lived alone in her own home, surrounded by people who had learned to stop seeing her.
